prompt: A worker's mean service time stays unchanged as utilisation rises close to full capacity. Under the M/M/1 model, why can a small further load increase cause a large response-time increase?

options.text: Requests spend much longer waiting for the worker, even though their own service time is unchanged
options.explanation: Correct. As spare capacity shrinks, random arrivals and service times create a sharply growing queue.

options.text: Each request necessarily requires more CPU instructions at higher utilisation
options.explanation: Incorrect. The scenario holds service time constant; waiting is the additional delay.

options.text: Response time must rise in direct proportion to utilisation
options.explanation: Incorrect. Near saturation the model's mean response time grows much more sharply than a proportional change.

options.text: Utilisation cannot affect response time if service time stays constant
options.explanation: Incorrect. Response time includes queueing as well as service.

workedExample: Separate time being served from time waiting. A request arriving behind busy work waits before its own service begins. Near full utilisation, the worker has little spare time to drain that backlog, so small load increases can cause large delays. The M/M/1 result depends on its random-arrival, random-service, single-server assumptions; real systems need measurements and queue limits.

prompt: A service meets its normal peak-utilisation target across three equally sized zones. It must also stay below a separate emergency utilisation limit after losing one zone. What must the capacity review do?

options.text: Check only normal utilisation; healthy headroom proves the outage case
options.explanation: Incorrect. Losing a zone removes capacity and shifts work to survivors.

options.text: Assume autoscaling replaces the lost zone instantly
options.explanation: Incorrect. Scaling has delays and may lack capacity during a regional incident.

options.text: Check the two surviving zones against peak traffic and measured latency at the emergency limit
options.explanation: Correct. Normal and failure conditions are separate constraints, and a utilisation limit alone does not guarantee acceptable latency.

options.text: Require the emergency utilisation limit to equal the normal target in every design
options.explanation: Incorrect. A product can choose different normal and degraded targets, provided they are explicit and validated.

workedExample: List the capacity available with all zones, then with one gone. Check the full peak load against each case and provision for the stricter requirement. If the failure policy allows higher utilisation, test its latency and overload behaviour rather than assuming it is safe.
